title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs
authors: Tasnin Tabassum Ali, Faisal Ahmed, Muhammad Anwarul Azim
abstract: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and five large language models (LLMs) evaluated zero-shot. From a corpus of 3798 patient records covering 20 specialties, we retained the five with the most records (Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, Gastroenterology) and split the resulting 2730 records 80:20 into training and test sets shared by all families. The best transformer was XLM-RoBERTa (86.26% accuracy, 86.21% macro-F1), the best ML model was SVM (84.98%, 84.92%), the best DL model was Bidirectional GRU (80.77%, 80.83%), and the best LLM was Gemini (90.29%, 90.15%). Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests show SVM significantly outperforming Bi-LSTM (adjusted p = 0.004), whereas the Gemini-versus-Grok gap does not survive correction (adjusted p = 0.104), and neither the strongest transformer versus the weakest LLM (Grok) nor SVM versus the strongest transformer reaches significance. A tuned classical model is thus statistically indistinguishable from the strongest transformer, so accuracy rankings alone should not be read as evidence of one family's superiority. The findings provide a comparative baseline for Bangla medical text classification.

infographic.key_insight: Gemini achieved the highest accuracy (90.29%), but SVM and the strongest transformer showed no statistically significant difference, cautioning against claims of model-family superiority.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Classifying informal Bangla patient narratives could support specialty referral workflows, but clinical utility and safety remain unproven.
method: Compared 6 classical ML models, 4 deep learning models, 4 fine-tuned transformers, and 5 zero-shot LLMs.
Used 2,730 patient records across Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, and Gastroenterology with a shared 80:20 train–test split.
Assessed performance and pairwise differences using Holm-corrected McNemar tests.
infographic.evidence_signal: Best-in-family accuracy was 90.29% for Gemini, 86.26% for XLM-RoBERTa, 84.98% for SVM, and 80.77% for Bidirectional GRU; the Gemini–Grok difference was not significant after correction.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covered only the five most represented specialties from a 20-specialty corpus, limiting generalization to broader referral settings.
infographic.paper_title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs

title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation
authors: Zeqiang Wang
abstract: Healthcare systems periodically revise diagnostic and procedural classifications (ICD-9 to ICD-10/11), update hospital reimbursement groupers (MS-DRG), and deploy clinical coding across languages. Supervised coding networks bind clinical text encoders to fixed per-code classifier weights, forcing hospitals to re-annotate tens of thousands of records before switching codebooks, whereas standalone large language models incur high latency and hallucinate invalid codes. Here we show that day-one clinical codebook switching becomes feasible without target-labeled notes when local clinical evidence reading is decoupled from a strictly frozen multilingual concept space. Laya-IsoToken trains a clinical span reader once on source records with zero per-code classifier parameters, separating text evidence from historical disease prevalence. Given only public target code descriptions, closed-form matrix compilation aligns distributional shifts, compensates for paraphrased definitions, and deduplicates sibling codes in under three seconds, while a pre-deployment geometric residual routes unfamiliar concepts to offline language model verification. Across 32,804 MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharges, Laya-IsoToken matches published supervised baselines (62.6% Micro-F1) while reducing active calibration error by 32%. Switched with zero target training notes to 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges, MS-DRG groups, and multilingual cohorts, it outperforms biomedical dense retrievers, semantic crosswalks (+5.4 F1 points on ICD-10, paired $d_z = 0.49$, $p < 0.001$), and official US CMS equivalence mappings (+3.5 points, $p < 0.001$) at 9.4 ms per admission. Pairing this reader with an offline 31B verifier across 1,000 full discharge summaries lifts zero-training ICD-10 coding to 40.6% Micro-F1 (57.0% category F1, $d_z = 0.66$, $p < 0.001$) with 0.0% invalid code hallucinations.

infographic.key_insight: Laya-IsoToken enables clinical codebook switching without target-labeled training notes by separating clinical text evidence from a frozen multilingual concept space.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could reduce reannotation burden when hospitals adopt new coding systems, reimbursement groupers, or languages.
method: Train a clinical span reader on source records without per-code classifier weights.
Compile public target code descriptions into alignment operators in under three seconds.
Use a geometric residual to flag unfamiliar concepts for offline language-model verification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on 32,804 ICD-9 and 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges, the system exceeded CMS mappings by 3.5 F1 points; adding an offline 31B verifier achieved 40.6% ICD-10 Micro-F1 with no invalid codes observed across 1,000 summaries.
infographic.watch_item: Zero invalid codes does not mean correct coding; moderate ICD-10 performance and offline verifier requirements warrant validation before operational use.
infographic.paper_title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation

title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
authors: Neda Ghafouri
abstract: As clinical AI agents begin to interact with electronic health records (EHRs), large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate their actions. But how reliably can these judges recognize clinically dangerous mistakes, especially when an agent appears to have completed its task successfully? We investigate this question using MedAgentBench by introducing controlled clinical errors into verified agent trajectories. The experiments include 416 faulty trajectories, eight error categories, and six open-weight LLM judges. By comparing each faulty trajectory with its correct counterpart, we measure whether judges genuinely recognize errors rather than simply flagging more actions as unsafe. The findings show that access to clinical evidence significantly improves judge reliability. When shown only the final answer, judges cannot distinguish errors that leave it unchanged, while flagging 56% of correct trajectories. With full trajectory information, the ability to distinguish unsafe actions from correct ones reaches a score of 0.75, and providing actual EHR responses improves discrimination by 0.39. Surprisingly, including the agent's reasoning does not improve overall performance and reduces detection of incorrectly reported clinical values by 0.18, which remain the hardest errors to detect. MedGemma performed worse than the general-purpose model and was the only judge to miss potentially dangerous medication overdoses. We also find that the benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with an intentionally skipped laboratory check, while combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults.

infographic.key_insight: LLM judges better distinguish unsafe clinical actions when given EHR evidence, while agent reasoning does not improve overall performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating EHR-connected AI agents requires checking clinical actions against patient records, not just assessing whether final answers appear correct.
method: Injected controlled errors across eight categories into verified MedAgentBench trajectories.
Evaluated six open-weight LLM judges on 416 faulty trajectories paired with correct counterparts.
Compared evidence access and combined LLM judgments with a full-EHR rule-based checker.
infographic.evidence_signal: Full-trajectory evaluation reached a discrimination score of 0.75; the original grader accepted all 38 skipped-lab-check trajectories, while combined LLM and rule-based checks detected 97% of injected faults.
infographic.watch_item: These benchmark results use injected errors and do not establish safety or reliability in real-world clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study

title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios
authors: Yera Choi, Yeong Hwa Kim, Jaedeok Lee, Taekang Kim, Sangdoo Yun, Seong-Eun Moon
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at medical question answering yet are rarely evaluated on the stepwise diagnostic reasoning that defines real clinical workflows, where impressions are revised as information accumulates. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information. Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further, exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment.

infographic.key_insight: ASCENT exposes a gap between answering fully specified medical questions and updating diagnostic reasoning as clinical information arrives.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark supports evaluation of reasoning in workflows resembling staged clinical assessment, without establishing readiness for patient care.
method: Constructed 3,078 clinician-annotated stepwise problems from MedQA-USMLE.
Organized vignettes into EMR-aligned Findings, Impression, and supporting Rationale steps.
Evaluated LLMs, fine-tuned Qwen2.5 models, and tested robustness to altered prior impressions and sequential rollout.
infographic.evidence_signal: ASCENT fine-tuning improved F1 for Qwen2.5-7B and 32B over pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, primarily through precision gains.
infographic.watch_item: Errors can propagate across sequential diagnostic steps, and exam-derived benchmark gains do not establish real-world clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios

title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval
authors: Guy Shmueli, Keno K. Bressem, Tom Hope
abstract: Retrieving images of patients clinically similar to a given patient can support diagnosis, teaching and research. Training and evaluating retrieval systems requires knowing which images of different patients show the same finding, and existing datasets are small or narrow in scope. We construct PMC-PaIR, a dataset of 86,144 pairs of clinically similar images from 56,013 open-access PubMed Central case reports, which often document rare or challenging presentations. We develop an approach that follows citations, which often link case reports of similar patients. To determine what two linked cases share clinically, it prompts large language models to generate and answer hierarchical questions, from modality to diagnosis and findings, and to match images by caption using the answers. Experts find the pairs highly accurate, and this question-guided approach finds twice as many correct pairs as direct matching. Fine-tuning BiomedCLIP on PMC-PaIR improves retrieval in all modality, anatomy and diagnosis categories tested, for image-only queries and image queries with a short text naming the finding. We release the dataset and the automated pipeline, which can extend PMC-PaIR as new case reports are published.

infographic.key_insight: Citation-linked case reports can yield clinically similar image pairs that improve medical image retrieval after model fine-tuning.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Retrieving images from clinically similar cases could support clinical reference, teaching and research, but diagnostic benefit was not established.
method: Follow citations between open-access PubMed Central case reports to identify potentially similar cases.
Use large language models to ask and answer hierarchical questions about modality, diagnosis and findings, then match images using captions.
Fine-tune BiomedCLIP on the resulting PMC-PaIR dataset.
infographic.evidence_signal: PMC-PaIR contains 86,144 image pairs from 56,013 case reports; experts judged pairs highly accurate, question-guided matching found twice as many correct pairs as direct matching, and fine-tuning improved retrieval across all tested categories.
infographic.watch_item: Case reports often feature rare or challenging presentations, so performance on routine clinical images requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval

title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
authors: Merel Kuijs, Till Richter, Rushin H. Gindra, Korbinian Traeuble, Christian Matek, Rebeka Luknárová
abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

infographic.key_insight: CAMEO learns shared multimodal representations from small, partially paired datasets, outperforming CLIP-like contrastive approaches when paired data are scarce.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support computational pathology research combining images and gene expression when matched samples are limited, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Uses pre-trained unimodal encoders.
Aligns modalities in a shared latent space through adversarial learning.
Requires only limited paired samples for multimodal fusion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on niche classification and cell type composition prediction, plus release of an annotated three-organ dataset with paired images and gene expression, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to independent clinical datasets and effects on patient care are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data

title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT
authors: Hanbin Ko, Hong-Jun Choi, Jihun Kim, Young-Gon Kim, Dongheon Lee, Chang Min Park
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.

infographic.key_insight: JECT addresses a context shortcut in chest CT learning by making the image encoder predict report content, rather than relying on surrounding anatomy to represent hidden findings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could improve representations for chest CT classification, finding localization, and risk prediction, but clinical utility remains to be established.
method: Condition masked-region feature prediction on the radiology report.
Train the encoder to predict masked anatomical report sections from the unmasked scan.
Use a hierarchical 3D encoder with prediction at every stage to retain clinical content across scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained from scratch on 173k CT volumes, JECT reportedly matched current CT foundation models on classification, retrieval, and nodule malignancy, and task-specific models on lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish prospective clinical performance or generalizability across institutions and report styles.
infographic.paper_title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT

title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
authors: Benedikt von Querfurth, Lukas Klein, Cédric Vincent-Cuaz, Eeshaan Jain, Yexiang Cheng, Johann Wenckstern
abstract: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.

infographic.key_insight: VirTues-M2 jointly learns tissue morphology and spatial protein patterns to support multiple cancer research tasks within one model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model could help link routine H&E images with molecular tissue features for prognostic research, but clinical utility remains to be established.
method: Uses a multimodal vision transformer to integrate H&E histopathology and multiplex spatial proteomics.
Encodes marker identity to accommodate variable marker panels, missing modalities, and imperfect pairing or registration.
Supports tissue phenotyping, cell segmentation, virtual staining, biomarker discovery, and adaptive marker selection.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive NSCLC patients with paired modalities, discovered tissue signatures stratified overall survival in discovery and independent validation cohorts, reportedly outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative performance estimates or prospective clinical evaluation, limiting assessment of effect size and deployment readiness.
infographic.paper_title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer

title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments
authors: Yang Bai, Yingzhi Xia, Ling Lin, Jun Cheng, Lin Fu, Huazhu Fu
abstract: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.

infographic.key_insight: Multimodal LLMs struggle with hospital spatial reasoning, while targeted fine-tuning and GeoJeV’s explicit 3D computation improve benchmark performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark tests abilities relevant to navigating hospital spaces and locating equipment, but does not establish safety or effectiveness in clinical use.
method: Created 3,368 questions across eight spatial task types using simulated walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts.
Evaluated 35 multimodal LLMs and fine-tuned two models on 44,750 training questions.
Developed GeoJeV to reconstruct 3D scene memory and incorporate evidence from question-selected spatial operations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Best open and proprietary models achieved 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy; physicians scored 79.0% on a subset, and GeoJeV ranked highest among evaluated models.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from simulated environments; robustness in real hospitals remains unproven, and supplying 3D maps alone did not ensure models used them.
infographic.paper_title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments

title: SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures
authors: Xinhe Wu, Yicheng Ye, Yadong Jin
abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.

infographic.key_insight: SciFig2Data converts scientific figures in PDFs into structured measurements linked to caption-derived experimental context.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The workflow could support biomedical evidence aggregation and AI research, but the abstract does not establish clinical utility.
method: Detect figures, separate panels, and filter content using OCR.
Classify charts with a Swin-based model and reconstruct tables using an instruction-guided multimodal model.
Associate measurements with caption metadata and enable batch processing with caching and logging.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 605 toxicology/pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle articles, the workflow reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports output counts but not numerical reconstruction accuracy, so recovered data require validation before downstream use.
infographic.paper_title: SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures

title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
authors: Ignazio Gallo, Mattia Gatti, Leonardo Sgroi, Darwin Castillo, Yuliana Jiménez-Gaona, Nicola Landro
abstract: Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above every imaging arm we evaluated (best 0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, reproduces every finding except legibility, from a confounder that is clinically legitimate. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.

infographic.key_insight: Patient-level splits prevent subject leakage but cannot rule out acquisition confounders that predict diagnosis across the entire dataset.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Strong medical imaging benchmark performance may reflect acquisition patterns rather than pathology, limiting confidence in clinical generalization.
method: Audit whether a candidate confounder predicts diagnosis and can be decoded from images.
Test whether diagnostic scores depend on it and whether images add predictive value beyond it.
Measure discrimination after controlling for the confounder.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 236 DMR-IR patients evaluated with patient-disjoint splits, acquisition date predicted malignancy at AUROC 0.980 versus 0.949 for the best imaging arm; no imaging arm improved on date alone in paired-fold comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Only eight cross-label same-date pairs from ten patients were available, preventing reliable assessment of pathology-specific discrimination within acquisition-date groups.
infographic.paper_title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark

title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
authors: Yitong Qiao, Lei Liu, Yue Shen, Jian Wang, Jinjie Gu, Zhixuan Chu
abstract: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states from screenshots and execute mouse-and-keyboard actions, as well as a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data. The environment verifies both final answers and required clinical actions, and supports parallel trajectory collection for training. Benchmarking twelve vision-language models shows that current agents struggle across diverse clinical workflows, and simply increasing reasoning effort fails to yield consistent gains. Furthermore, MedUIGym supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards. After training, both Qwen3.5 models perform better on in-domain clinical tasks and generalize to tasks from external sources. By unifying tasks from existing benchmarks, dual-interface evaluation, and GUI trajectory collection, MedUIGym provides a testbed for studying how vision-language agents complete clinical tasks through the EHR's graphical interface. Our project page is available at https://github.com/yitong-qiao/MedUIGym.

infographic.key_insight: MedUIGym provides a testbed for clinical GUI agents, showing that current models struggle with EHR workflows while task-based training improves performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The platform supports research on EHR workflow automation but does not establish safety or effectiveness in clinical practice.
method: Unifies clinical tasks in an interactive EHR environment with screenshot-based mouse-and-keyboard control.
Pairs GUI and native-tool interfaces over identical clinical data, verifying answers and required actions.
Supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation spans 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families and 12 vision-language models; both trained Qwen3.5 models improved on in-domain tasks and generalized to external-source tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark gains do not establish reliable performance across real-world EHR systems or patient-care settings.
infographic.paper_title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows

title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
authors: Nonchev, K.; Jang, Y.; Nlandu Khodo, S.; Koelzer, V. H.; Raetsch, G.; Moor, M. B.
abstract: IntroductionSpatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. MethodsWe adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1 534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. ResultsKidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each models 1 000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). In our atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots, higher proximal tubule program scores were associated with higher eGFR (partial r, 0.32) and less interstitial fibrosis (-0.57), and program-pathology associations agreed with those of measured Visium profiles in independent participants (Spearman{rho} , 0.64). ConclusionsKidney-adapted virtual spatial transcriptomics links histology-derived molecular programs to experimental renal injury and human clinical and histologic phenotypes. Our approach enables spatial molecular analyses in routine biopsy histology, which could help decipher disease-associated pathways in existing biopsy archives. Translational StatementSpatial molecular profiling of kidney biopsies is informative but too costly for routine use, whereas hematoxylin and eosin sections exist for nearly every biopsy. We show that a model adapted to paired kidney histology and spatial transcriptomics infers programs of tubular injury, metabolic differentiation, and fibrosis from routine histology, and that these programs track kidney function and pathology across 476 participants. Applied to existing archives, virtual spatial transcriptomics could stratify heterogeneous patients by tissue molecular state, prioritize biopsies for targeted assays, and support biomarker discovery and trial enrichment once validated prospectively.

infographic.key_insight: Kidney-adapted AI predicted spatial gene expression from routine histology, linking tissue appearance to disease-associated molecular programs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Virtual molecular profiling could extend research on kidney injury and function to archived biopsies without additional spatial transcriptomics assays.
method: Adapted DeepSpot-M using paired histology and Visium data from 209 KPMP participants.
Evaluated held-out human biopsies and injury associations in 567 rats without rat-specific training.
Generated 5.46 million virtual spots from 1,534 slides across 476 additional KPMP participants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Mean gene-expression correlation doubled from 0.22 to 0.43 for each model’s 1,000 best-predicted genes; predictions preserved all 13 tested disease-marker differences and all 11 measured eGFR associations.
infographic.watch_item: These predicted molecular profiles require prospective clinical validation and should not be treated as measured gene expression or established diagnostic tests.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs

title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
authors: Junbo Shen
abstract: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

infographic.key_insight: SAE-Audit improves clinical-trial outcome predictions by giving black-box LLMs concept-level evidence derived from an open model.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More accurate predictions of trial completion or early termination could support research planning, but do not establish treatment safety or efficacy.
method: Convert a frozen sparse autoencoder on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct into a vocabulary of clinical concepts.
Fit sparse probes on past trials to identify outcome-associated concepts.
Provide detected concepts and their association direction and strength to guide the target LLM’s answer.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports balanced-accuracy gains of 9.6–12.0 percentage points for deepseek-v4-flash across five trial-prediction tasks and 8.0 points for GPT-5.6-terra on trial completion.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify dataset sizes or external validation, leaving generalizability to new trial settings uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence

title: CT-Navigator: Towards Interpretable and Generalizable CT Understanding through Agentic Perception and Tool-Invocation
authors: Yibing Fu, Huidong Xie, Yihao Niu, Wei Ji, Heming Dong, Ziyue Wang
abstract: Clinical computed tomography (CT) interpretation inherently requires progressive visual exploration, where radiologists navigate from whole scans to individual slices and regions of interest and interact with external tools when necessary. However, existing 3D medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically connect a specialized 3D visual encoder to a language model, without fully leveraging the native 2D visual and agentic capabilities of generalist MLLMs. Trained on large-scale one-hop CT instruction-following data, these models also have limited ability to perform iterative reasoning and explicitly ground their conclusions in visual evidence, limiting their support for traceable CT interpretation. To solve these problems, we propose \textbf{agentic perception} as an alternative paradigm inspired by radiologists' interpretation workflows. We introduce \textbf{CT-Navigator}, a framework that harnesses generalist MLLMs' 2D visual and agentic capabilities to progressively ground CT interpretation in explicit, traceable visual evidence through hierarchical visual exploration and radiology tool invocation. To build these capabilities, we curate 8,904 visual chain-of-thought (V-CoT) trajectories for cold-start agentic supervised fine-tuning. We then optimize the policy through reinforcement learning on 33,219 questions, with data selection and dynamic rollout sampling prioritizing informative learning signals. Finally, we introduce CTNavi-Bench, a 3D CT visual question answering benchmark comprising 7,000 questions spanning anatomical regions throughout the human body. CT-Navigator achieves 79.50\% accuracy on CTNavi-Bench, surpassing the strongest baseline by 17.59\%, and demonstrates strong generalization across three external CT benchmarks. The code, model, and benchmark will be released on \href{https://github.com/fyb99/ct_navigator}{GitHub}.

infographic.key_insight: CT-Navigator uses generalist multimodal AI to explore CT scans progressively and invoke radiology tools, grounding answers in traceable visual evidence.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more transparent CT interpretation, but the abstract does not establish safety or effectiveness in clinical practice.
method: Navigate from whole scans to individual slices and regions of interest.
Train with 8,904 visual chain-of-thought trajectories for agentic supervised fine-tuning.
Apply reinforcement learning on 33,219 questions, prioritizing informative training signals.
infographic.evidence_signal: CT-Navigator achieved 79.50% accuracy on the new 7,000-question CTNavi-Bench, with a reported 17.59% gain over the strongest baseline and strong generalization across three external CT benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark performance and traceable visual evidence do not establish clinical reliability; prospective workflow validation remains necessary.
infographic.paper_title: CT-Navigator: Towards Interpretable and Generalizable CT Understanding through Agentic Perception and Tool-Invocation

title: When Should We Trust Medical Image Models? Evaluating Confidence Reliability under Cross-Dataset Shift
authors: Haoran Zhang, Sarah Lam, Yuting Lin, Nuo Chen, Mingyang Li
abstract: Deep learning models for chest X-ray analysis often achieve strong performance on benchmark datasets, but their reliability under cross-dataset deployment remains unclear. In clinical practice, models trained in one hospital system may be applied to data from another, where distributional and labeling differences can affect both prediction accuracy and model confidence. We conduct a controlled empirical study of model confidence under cross-dataset transfer. We train ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121 on CheXpert and evaluate them on MIMIC-CXR across five experimental settings, focusing on Pneumothorax and Pleural Effusion. We measure predictive performance using AUC and confidence reliability using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Brier score, and average confidence on incorrect predictions, all reported with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. We further evaluate post-hoc temperature scaling fit on the source validation set and use Grad-CAM to examine the mechanism behind cross-domain performance differences. Cross-domain AUC drops 7-13 percentage points, and the best in-domain model is not the best cross-domain model. Source-domain temperature scaling produces marginal ECE changes but systematically increases confidence on incorrect predictions across all four model-pathology combinations. Grad-CAM reveals that DenseNet relies on a concentrated spatial prior that fails to transfer, while ResNet's more distributed attention generalizes better. These findings argue for cross-site validation and safety-specific calibration metrics in medical AI evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Strong benchmark performance did not ensure reliable cross-dataset predictions, and source-fitted temperature scaling increased confidence in errors.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Chest X-ray AI may become less accurate and misleadingly confident when transferred between hospital datasets, supporting cross-site validation before deployment.
method: Trained ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121 on CheXpert; evaluated transfer to MIMIC-CXR for pneumothorax and pleural effusion.
Measured AUC, ECE, Brier score, and average confidence on incorrect predictions with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
Tested source-validation temperature scaling and examined attention patterns using Grad-CAM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five experimental settings, cross-domain AUC fell 7–13 percentage points, while temperature scaling increased confidence on errors in all four model–pathology combinations.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence covers two architectures, two findings, and one dataset-transfer direction; broader clinical generalizability remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: When Should We Trust Medical Image Models? Evaluating Confidence Reliability under Cross-Dataset Shift

title: A Cascaded Framework with a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN Model for Pre- and Post-Treatment Glioma Segmentation
authors: Siavash Taremi, Mahmoud Heidari, Seyed Mohammad Hossein Hashemi, Mohsen Hooshmand
abstract: Accurate glioma segmentation is vital for diagnosis and follow-up, but manual segmentation is time-consuming, subjective, and variable across interpreters. Gliomas are heterogeneous in size, shape, and location. Deep learning has therefore emerged as a potential solution. CNNs excel at local features but may struggle with long-range dependencies, whereas Vision Transformers capture global context efficiently but incur higher computational complexity. Most previous studies focused on pre-treatment gliomas; post-treatment cases with resection cavities (RCs) remain less explored. This study proposes a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN (CMC-Seg) model within a cascaded framework for pre- and post-treatment diffuse glioma segmentation, aiming to balance accuracy and computational cost. Experiments used BraTS 2025 mpMRI of diffuse glioma patients. After preprocessing, a coarse segmentation model extracted tumor-centered patches, which were fed to CMC-Seg for fine-grained segmentation. CMC-Seg was compared with 3D U-Net, SegResNet, SwinUNETR, UNETR, nnFormer, and SegMamba. On the test set, CMC-Seg achieved the highest mean Dice (81.20%) and non-enhancing tumor core (NETC) Dice (77.09%). It also achieved an RC Dice of 78.63% and the lowest 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95; 4.39 mm). Results were comparable to CNN and Mamba baselines and significantly better than Transformer-based baselines (P < 0.05). CMC-Seg required the fewest inference GFLOPs (381.49). Ablation experiments indicated that multi-direction scanning and cross-attention improved performance, particularly for RC (P < 0.05). Grad-CAM explainability experiments showed that CMC-Seg focuses on diagnostically relevant tumor regions.

infographic.key_insight: CMC-Seg combined Mamba and CNN features to achieve the highest mean Dice (81.20%) and lowest inference GFLOPs (381.49) among evaluated models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Automated segmentation of pre- and post-treatment gliomas, including resection cavities, could support imaging assessment, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: A coarse model identified tumor-centered patches from preprocessed multiparametric MRI.
CMC-Seg refined segmentation using a cross-attention-guided Mamba-CNN architecture.
Ablations assessed multi-direction scanning and cross-attention.
infographic.evidence_signal: On BraTS 2025 test data, CMC-Seg achieved 77.09% NETC Dice, 78.63% resection-cavity Dice, and 4.39 mm HD95, with performance comparable to CNN/Mamba baselines and significantly better than Transformer baselines (P < 0.05).
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report external validation or clinical workflow testing, so real-world generalizability and practical efficiency remain uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: A Cascaded Framework with a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN Model for Pre- and Post-Treatment Glioma Segmentation

title: KMed-31B Technical Report
authors: KMed Team
abstract: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD$^2$). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.

infographic.key_insight: KMed-31B combines task-specialist training with multi-teacher distillation to improve medical dialogue benchmark scores while maintaining or slightly improving multiple-choice medical performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support institutions developing on-premises medical language models, but benchmark gains do not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
method: Divide medical tasks into four categories by expected output and available feedback, then train a specialist for each.
Build Synthetic Health Dialogue from simulated consultations covering common primary-care presentations.
Integrate specialists into one student using Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD²).
infographic.evidence_signal: In thinking mode, HealthBench Hard rose from 23.80 to 51.48 and Professional from 41.97 to 59.18; four multiple-choice benchmark scores were maintained or slightly improved, and the recipe also improved another base model.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports benchmark evaluations rather than prospective clinical deployment; real-world safety and local hardware requirements need validation.
infographic.paper_title: KMed-31B Technical Report

title: Biomechanically Grounded Prediction of Selective Motor Control and Clinical Outcomes from Infant Video
authors: Divya Joshi, Ruize Yang, Colleen Peyton, R. James Cotton
abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy

infographic.key_insight: Biomechanically grounded 3D joint-angle estimates from single-camera infant videos enabled AI prediction of selective motor control scores and separation of infants with versus without cerebral palsy.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support scalable infant movement assessment, but its cerebral palsy discrimination remained below expert clinician scoring.
method: BB3D estimates infant 3D joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video.
A spatio-temporal transformer was pretrained on 1,000+ recordings and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants.
The model predicts individual BabyOSCAR items and total scores without training on diagnosis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation showed 17.5 mm median aligned joint-center error in 17 infants; on held-out recordings, BabyOSCAR total correlation was 0.86, while cerebral palsy discrimination AUC was 0.86 versus 0.67 for a 2D baseline and 0.97 for expert scores.
infographic.watch_item: Within-site evaluation and a small 3D validation cohort leave cross-site generalizability and clinical implementation uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Biomechanically Grounded Prediction of Selective Motor Control and Clinical Outcomes from Infant Video

title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
authors: Inigo Stibbe, Padmanabhan Ramnarayan, A. Aldo Faisal
abstract: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

infographic.key_insight: Synthetic EHR generators should undergo patient-level memorisation audits, since similarity heuristics and aggregate metrics can obscure privacy risks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These audits could help assess whether synthetic clinical records expose information memorised from individual patients.
method: Compare membership-inference evaluations across four autoregressive EHR generators.
Test patient-trajectory reconstruction from partial context.
Use randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorisation from clinical generalisation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, training-patient canaries were systematically recovered and reconstruction approached perfect accuracy as context increased, unlike held-out patients.
infographic.watch_item: This deliberately overfit positive control demonstrates audit sensitivity, not the prevalence of memorisation in realistically trained models.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
